title.narrative: Skilling in Agripreneurship for increased Youth Employment - SAY Project

description.narrative: AVSI is implementing a 4 Years project – Till end of 2024 funded by the Embassy of the Kingdom of Netherlands titled “Skilling in Agripreneurship for increased Youth Employment” – SAY project. The project will contribute to: Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands 2019-2024 Multi Year Strategic Plan, Vision 2040 of Uganda, Uganda National Agriculture Policy 2013 and the BTVET 10-year Strategic Plan for Revolutionizing Skills Development in Uganda (Skilling Uganda Initiative) with a focus on youth.It will furthermore contribute to the following Sustainable Development Goals: #1 No Poverty, #2 Zero Hunger, #5 Gender Equality, #7 Affordable and Clean Energy, #8 Decent Work and Economic Growth, #13 Climate Action, #15 Life On Land, #16 Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions, #17 Partnerships for the Goals and will have a tangible impact to Uganda’s SDG report card.

The SAY Goal is: To contribute to increased agri-skills level and gainful employment of youth in the agriculture sector in UgandaThe specific objectives are as follows: Specific Objective 1: Employable agribusiness skills levels of 18,800 youth 18-30 years old in target areas in Uganda enhanced by 2024.Specific Objective 2: Skilled youth (aged 18-30 years) employment in well-paying agribusiness jobs and self-run agripreneurship in target project areas of Uganda boosted by the end of the project (2024)Specific Objective 3: 6,500 Youth aged 13 <18 years in target project areas of Uganda increased their engagement in agriculture for long-term career path or key economic venture by the end of project (2024)Specific Objective 4: Enabling environment for market-responsive agri-skilling and youth gainful engagement in agribusiness in Uganda strengthened by 2024

comment.narrative: There are reform processes in line with job creation and agri-skilling which have been proposed under the Skilling Uganda Initiative, TVET Policy of 2019 and the National Strategy for Youth Employment in Agriculture (NSYEA).

In 2021, the SAY project targeted to collaborate with the Ministries of Agriculture Animal Industry and Fisheries, Ministry of Gender Labour and Social Development, and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) to popularize the NSYEA and earn the buy in of the private sector actors to engage in agri-skilling and creation of jobs in the agriculture sector. The project also targeted engaging the Directorate of Industrial Training (DIT) of the Ministry of Education and Sports for reforms in assessment and certification to make it more responsive to the circumstances on the ground.

In 2021, after the joint regional awareness creation and popularization drives of the NSYEA conducted by AVSI, FAO, MAAIF and MGLSD, the role of private sector actors in the implementation of NSYEA was included in the policy document and implementation framework and forwarded to the National Planning Authority for endorsement and confirmation.The DIT was able to agree on proposed reformed to have industrial actors nominate assessors for occupations for which DIT doesn't have pre-selected assessors. This reform has eased the assessment waiting time for youth after completion of training.

title.narrative: OP 2.1.1: Youth started and run their own agribusinesses as full time employment

description.narrative: Capacitating youth agribusinesses into strong commercial businesses which create value to the products produced in a sustainable manner, supporting the inclusion of youth in lucrative value chains, connecting youth and facilitating their active participation in modern agricultural markets, and facilitating linkages to financing mechanisms will result into OR 2.1.1. The project will develop capacities of youth in entrepreneurship, business planning and management to start and operate sustainable viable agribusinesses. The project will as well broker the development of stable and equal commercial relations throughout the whole chain. These relations will lead to a better integration of youth within the different links of the chain in order to satisfy market demands and market opportunities induced by modernization of agricultural chains and a more equal distribution of benefits and risks between the different chain actors. The project will also support youth engagement in forward integration through supporting access to business incubation services so that they add value to products and sell them further down the chains, domestically, regionally and internationally. The market chain development model that the project will promote makes use of identifying markets and zooming into specific buyers. Identified demand will be linked to production areas after which joint market chains will be established. The SAY project will play an important role in the identification of these potential buyers/markets and support more inclusive procurement strategies and practices in order to give youth the possibility to participate in highly modern markets as a trigger to become highly competitive businesses in national/ regional markets. These linkages will result in direct market access to domestic, regional and international export markets by youth. Also, through multi stakeholder processes, the project will influence chain actors in the targeted chains to share a common vision and objectives on fair trade, create synergies and develop sustainable products with youth. Additionally, it will endeavor to identify and interest key support institutions such as agri-finance and credit institutions to provide services to the youth businesses. The project will also design booster packages as well as set up challenge funds to provide alternative financing mechanisms. The project will employ a mix of market systems development approaches, all geared towards creating a demand pull from the consumers. Under this project, particular emphasis will be given to Making Market Work for the Poor (M4P) and Value Chain Development (VCD).

title.narrative: Output (OP)1.1.1: Youth attended training in technical and soft agribusiness skills

description.narrative: For youth to get into either self-employment or wage employment they need to have sets of skills to be able to execute the given task. Under this project hands on technical and soft skills will be provided to the youth to enable them to compete favorably in the market. The technical skills in selected occupations will be provided by competent instructors who will use the reviewed and developed Assessment and Training Packages (ATPs) at level 2 and 3. The project will integrate soft and job readiness skills like ICT, communication, financial literacy, business planning, negotiation, work ethics, marketing, report writing critical thinking, problem solving among others into the training curriculum to enable them make meaningful contribution to their employers and businesses. The capacity of skills providers/instructors will be built through trainings and exposures to enable them provide up to date skills to the youth. The project will use mixed approaches to provide competent based skills to the youth. In the project youth will be trained onsite, off site and online. There will be a number of exposures visits to successful youth established farms and platforms for knowledge and information sharing as well as networking and linkages. Exceptional youth will be supported in national competition for competitive funding. In addition, for continuous and sustained learning, the project will support the establishment and functionality of BTVET/University business incubation hubs. An alumni association for the incubation hub will be formed to facilitate experience sharing and learning.

title.narrative: SO2: Skilled youth (aged 18-30 years) employment in well-paying agribusiness jobs and self-run agripreneurship in target project areas of Uganda boosted by the end of the project (2024)

description.narrative: From the experience of SKY majority of the youth, at least 79% showed preference for self-employment. Even those engaged in waged employment had plans of engaging in agripreneurship. This has guided the strategy in the new project where more 70% of the youth will be skilled and facilitated to get into self-employment. For this reason, 2 pathways into employment will be executed, one for self-employment (agripreneurship) and the other for wage employment. Wage employment will be prioritized for youth with higher education level as they will have the competitive ability in the job market compared to those with lower educational levels. Self-employment will be open for all youth across the board. The first strategy will be to map all companies engaged in the lucrative upper nodes of the chain who are able to engage in skilling or integrating the skilled youth as part of their supply chain or as employees.For youth going into self-employment, their package will include skilling in entrepreneurship, soft skills and the technical aspects of the agripreneurship they are primed for, agribusiness incubation and development services including support from PUM experts, opportunity to compete for the agribusiness challenge fund grant, linking to a big actor in the value chain for off-take and access to investment capital, and business formalization support. A market-driven approach will be designed to address bottle-necks that hinder access to lucrative market opportunities by the youth. This category of youth will be introduced to value chains as contracted supply chain contributors or agents of big companies to disseminate agro-inputs/products and offer after-sales services. External markets in South Sudan, Rwanda and Kenya will be targeted for the self-employed youth. The youth skilled under SKY 1 will form the first cohort for upgrading/retooling in this category. Occupations at level 2 and 3 will be the priority entry point for youth targeted for wage employment (at agribusiness companies). The big agribusinesses engaged in the selected value chain enterprises will be mapped out and partnered with through the multi-stakeholder platforms to take in the final year youth from Universities and Colleges for internship/apprenticeship placement and retain a certain quota as their employees. Job Brokerage through the job connection platforms is another strategy that will be executed to get the youth into well-paying jobs. Occupational health and safety is another priority aspect that will be addressed for youth to be employed by companies. The project will conduct career awareness sessions for university/college finalist students to enable them understand how early-career jobs fit into a career trajectory and thus prepare for their first job experience. Work readiness skills training will be the main service package for wage employed youth and will be delivered in a phased manner with engagement of agribusiness staff and matching capacity needs of the youth.SKY staff will actively participate in the enrolment of the youth to ensure that only those with the desired attributes are enrolled into the project. This is a critical objective on which one of the key outcomes of the project that is of national importance (reduction of youth unemployment) directly hinges on. If the post-skilling support pays off this objective will be achieved to a magnitude dependent on IO 2.1.

title.narrative: SO3: Youth aged 13 <18 years in target project areas of Uganda increased their engagement in agriculture for long-term career path or key economic venture by the end of project (2024)

description.narrative: Getting the young people of school-going age to engage in agribusiness is key for the future of the agriculture sector. So the intervention in schools and remand homes is aiming at increasing the number of youth in agribusiness or agriculture occupations. by promoting agriculture as a viable career and income generation option among the youth 13<18 years. As a strategy for promoting positive mindset change among youth 13<18 years, the project will seek to expose youth to learning opportunities that demonstrate the wide range of opportunities within agribusiness to stimulate interest and innovation. This will be done by unpacking agriculture in such a way that demystifies the subject that has been relegated to an elective subject in the new curriculum and promote it as a subject of choice among the students. This will set a foundation for the future workforce in agribusiness as well as foster new agripreneurshipsResults from SKY indicated an increased number of students choosing agriculture and this is expected to further increase with the implementation of the new project.The implementation in schools will be through the student agribusiness clubs building on the success of SKY and paying specific attention harmonizing interventions with the new curriculum with regard to assessment and certification. All skills attained by the students under the project intervention will be certified by DIT to ensure skills and competencies are built from early stages of the youth career in agribusiness. The main proposed programming strategies, models and approaches for this objective (SO3) will be:a)Hands-on knowledge and skills transfer:AVSI proposes to invest in practical session learning sites in targeted schools for the youth in schools to learn agricultural and entrepreneurial skills and appreciate their productive outcome when put into use. These learning sites run by highly trained facilitators will run as centers of excellence where by youth skilled by the project are deployed to facilitate clinics in different topics of interest for other youth from other schools or nearby communities. This will create a snowball effect that will engage more youth in agribusiness ventures, thus amplifying the project’s impact and increase youth engagement in agriculture. b)Promotion of youth-led Innovations:Youth will be supported under the new phase to engage in selected lucrative enterprises that present the best business opportunities. The new phase will be designed to involve the strong private sector players in skilling youth at agri-institutions to influence the delivery model of agri-institutions towards being market oriented.AVSI will engage with agri-institutions to allocate the finalists part of the infrastructure to facilitate learning with production model and facilitate finalist youths and the institutions to engage in business transactions. The youth will be able to generate capital for self-start up or linked to available opportunities for wage employment.c)Exposure and networking:Exposing the youth to the dimensions of agriculture and various nodes of the value chain so that they can see and appreciate the importance and value of agriculture to individual and community socio-economic transformation. When the young people see the amount of money that change hands along the value chains there is a high chance that they will be inspired and attracted. Introducing the young people to networks of value chain actors will be an inspirational and eye-opening opportunity for them to draw closer to agriculture and become protagonists too. d)Climate and environment compliant innovations:In the next phase, the project will focus on waste management. The project proposes to build the capacity of youth in agri-institutions to produce briquettes from food and farm wastes (Banana peels, coffee husks, maize, cassava paste, etc) and briqette saving stoves for domestic use, restaurants, schools and chicken brooders. The youth will produce honey comb briquettes that have a very high efficiency and produce a very good flame. The project will facilitate trained youth and women to start business in briquette making and develop outlets for briquettes and stoves in different parts of the country. the project will also support youth to design new stove/energy products for selected businesses such as chicken brooders for poultry farms.e)Partnership with Children Remand Homes and Rehabilitation Center:AVSI will sign MoUs with remand homes to impart employable agribusiness skills to youth during their time at the remand homes. An adapted Earn As You Learn model will be applied to ensure that the youth earn some income and acquire startup that will allow them have a beginning to integrate back into society.

title.narrative: SO4: Enabling environment for market-responsive agri-skilling and youth gainful engagement in agribusiness in Uganda strengthened by 2024

description.narrative: In order for youth skilled under the SAY project to gain access to lucrative employment opportunities or commodity markets, stakeholders/actors have facilitation roles to play and mechanisms to put in place and operationalize. In essence, the youth need an enabling environment for them to attain their full potential in agribusiness as employees or agripreneurs. An enabling environment combines macro-economic policies that favour markets and trade, the provision of inputs, related physical infrastructure (such as roads and irrigation) and social infrastructure (such as ‎‎education and research). Creating the desired enabling environment for youth engagement in agriculture requires leadership and the engagement of all key stakeholders given the complex challenges facing the sector around the world, especially in emerging markets like Uganda. The Agriculture Growth Enabling Index (AGEI) lists 4 main components of the enabling environment that must be prioritized for interventions especially in emerging economies like Uganda. These components are governance (policy frameworks, regulations and value chain power mandates), capital (human, financial and other resources), markets and agriculture factors (inputs, production systems, climate etc) . These components are well incorporated and prioritized in the Uganda Agriculture Policy 2013 and the National Development Plan III. Governments in any country are primary duty bearers who play pivotal roles in creating an enabling environment for agricultural development. By providing a stable policy environment and avoiding unpredictable policy shifts, poor regulatory transparency, weak contract enforcement or restrictive investment policies, farmers can be supported to productively and beneficially engage in trading activities. A supportive enabling environment depends not only on the presence of laws and regulation, but their implementation; in agriculture, this requires strong political support for the sector at the highest levels. The role of private sector in economic development is undoubtedly critical. This is because 90% of the labour force in low and middle income economies are employed by the private sector and the sector controls the lion share of key agricultural resources such as land, financial capital and markets. They SAY project proposes public-private partnerships in the agriculture ecosystem in Uganda to support efforts to bring about reforms in the enabling environment. This will be done through support to government bodies to implement policies reforms and plans focused on enhance the 4 components of AGEI. The project will also facilitate the participation of private sector actors in the reform interventions and advocate for their long-term commitment to contribute to the various processes aimed at improving employability of youth in the agriculture sector and creation of opportunities and mechanisms that will enhance the youth’s access to employment, investment capital, agricultural inputs and commodity markets. Achieving specific objective (SO) 4 will have a ripple effect on the other SOs as the outcome of SO4 is foundation on which the other outcomes of the project stand. The strategy to achieve an improved enabling environment will include but not limited to:a)Enterprise support services:AVSI will map out all potential enterprise support organizations (ESOs) and provide this information to all the skilled youths for easy access to financial support. This AVSI will do through a designated private sector actor to establish formal collaboration with the identified partners. Under SKY, the Uganda Agribusiness Alliance (UAA) played this role and brought actors together and youths were able to benefit from the initiative. b)Collaboration with the public sector:AVSI recognizes that the public sector holds the mandate to carry out socio-economic development activities and that what development partners do is a contribution to this mandate. Having public institutions on board comes with several benefits that includes strategic and critical technical guidance, access to other opportunities, co-ownership of interventions and policy guidance. Under SKY project AVSI collaborated with Ministries of Education and Agriculture through their various Agencies and Departments. For the new project AVSI proposes to bring Ministry of Gender Labour and Social Development on board so that some inroads can be made into the labour market and create favourable enabling environment for youth to engage in agribusiness.c)Facilitation of ASSC:AVSI proposes to continue supporting the agriculture sector skills council by facilitating their activities and work plan. The ASSC still has pending activities in their 2016-2020 workplan that would not be fully implemented due to the disbandment of the Reform Taskforce and delay in operationalizing the TVET Council. d)Direct Engagement with Employers:A more formal collaboration between agri-institutions and employers/ private sector through MOUs will be up scaled in the next phase of the project. AVSI will map out all potential employers who can offer employer led skills and link them with the Agri-institutions for sustainable and long-term collaborationse)Participatory Learning:AVSI proposes to set a joint learning agenda between EKN, AVSI and targeted research institutions to increase the knowledge base on skills development and employment creation in the agriculture sector. The learning agenda will include action research that will be scientific and approved by the National Council of Science and Technology

title.narrative: SO Ind 4a: % of supported systemic and policy reforms that have led quality improvement in market-responsive agri-skilling

description.narrative: This indicator tracks the percentage number of supported policy and systemic reform processes that resulted in agri-skilling quality improvement divided by the total number of policy and systemic reform processes supported by the project

comment.narrative: SAY project has worked with MAAIF, MGLSD and MoES to support the implementation of the NSYEA (National Strategy for Youth Employment in Agriculture), National Youth Policy (NYP)and TVET (Technical and Vocational Education Training) Policy respectively.

In 2021, the SAY project targeted 2 systemic reform process that would lead to quality improvements into market responsive agri-skilling. One of these was the adjustments in the assessment and certification calendar and assignment of assessors of competences of the skilled youth. AVSI successfully dialogued with Directorate of Industrial Training to have skills providers provide their own assessors in instances where DIT do not have qualified accessors for specific value chains and occupations. The proposed assessors by the skills providers had to undergo validation by DIT and orientation on the assessment process. The second systemic reform process targeted in 2021 was the involvement of the Directorate of Human Resources and Extension in the skilling of Extension Workers who would later be considered for absorption in the Government Extension system.

The DIT was able to adjust the assessment and certification calendar to monthly and allowed assessors proposed by skills providers to assess the competencies of skilled youth. This resulted in ensuring assessment was conducted on time at the end of the skilling cycle.Ministry of Agriculture activity participated in the training of extension workers (Plant Doctors) who were subsequently absorbed in the extension system of the government and are now waiting to be assigned budgetary votes in District budget after which they will start work in their respective localities as government extension workers.

comment.narrative: AVSI conducted a contextual analysis survey internally as part of the roll-out process of the project and most importantly to enable the establishment of benchmarks against which to measure progress, determine baselines for some population level/systemic key performance indicators and to assess/identify potential partners and collaborators to engage in the project. The CAS sampled 393 youth aged 18-30 years, 144 youth aged 13<18 years (116 in schools and 28 in rehabilitation centers), 21 employers, 26 skills providers, 10 secondary schools, 5 line Ministries/Departments/Agencies, 4 private sector enablers, 4 CSOs and 1 donor agency. With 98% response rate and findings computed at a confidence level of 95% for quantitative data and attainment of response saturation by the 20th respondent for qualitative data, the results of the CAS is generalizable for the variables covered. Engagement in skills training:38% of youth 18-30 years are currently or in the past 1 year pursued studies, skills training or apprenticeship69% of the students 13<18 years are studying agriculture as an examinable subject while 31% are not. More male students study agriculture 93% compared to 59% of females. For children in conflict with the law, 82% were engaged in some form of agriculture before admission to the rehabilitation programme The 26 skills providers’ survey are engaged in skilling covering various occupations in the 4 sub-sectors of agriculture and at different occupation levels. Most of the skills providers offer skilling at levels 1 (78%) and 2 (81%) mainly with only 41% covering level 3 and 30% in level 4 occupation skilling. All the 10 surveyed schools have school farm/production units in which livestock, crops and agroforestry production and value addition processes take place. All the schools except Gayaza High School (does not have Agriculture at A level) offer Agriculture as an examinable subject at both Ordinary and Advanced levels and current student enrolment for the subjectSkills Training Delivery:The skilling centres mainly use 4 skills delivery methods with all of them conducting practical hands-on sessions; 70% using coaching, mentorship and job shadowing; 74% using the instructor-led classroom model and 11% conduct online sessions. Hands-on practical session is the predominant skilling model across all the nodes of the agriculture value chains followed by instructor-led classroom sessions, coaching/mentorship/job-shadowing, and online sessionsSecondary schools use 3 main models for agriculture training namely practical in school farms/production units, classroom theory and learning visits at a rate of at least 80% for each providing very suitable all-round training for the studentsDuration of skilling cycles:The trainings/skilling cycles were found to be 4.48 months long on average. The longest at 12 months for the Agriculturalists trained at Agricultural Colleges and the shortest at 1 months for some occupations skilled for by AgribusinessesSkilling Costs:The average costs for (excluding DIT assessment fees) was found to be UGX720,591/-. The skilling cost for each youth ranged from UGX120,000/- for a month-long non-residential training in food processing to UGX2,500,000/- for level 3 training in Dairy Value Addition. Assessment and Certification by DIT:16% (19% female, 13% male) were found to have been assessed and 97% passed by the DIT. All were old former beneficiaries of the SKY project.Demand/Interest in Agripreneurship among the youth97% of the youth (with insignificant variation between male and female preferences) indicated that they are interested in acquiring the skills and knowledge in agripreneurship89% indicated interest in technical skills compared to 44% that registered interests in soft skills The youth in rehabilitation were found to be interested in entrepreneurship skills (43%), practical agronomic skills (36%), life skills (25%), and future skills such as in IT (14%) that they will use when they are discharged. Involvement in Agripreneurship:Youth 18-30 years, 75% (78% females, 73% males) were engaged in agriculture in various value chains and levels with 72% engaged in crops, 48% in livestock and 2% each in agroforestry and aquaculture. 82% of youth in rehabilitation centres were engaged in agriculture before admission. For youth 13<18 years in schools, 79% (81% female, 74% male) were stated that they were currently engaged in agriculture ventures either at home, at school13<18 years’ youth earnings from agripreneurshipYouth undergoing rehabilitation at Naguru Remand Home who indicated that they were engaged in agriculture earned an average of UGX 776,111/- per yearFor the youth in secondary schools, their earning from engagement in agriculture averaged UGX771,019/= per years from the venturesYouth employment (18-30 years category):45% employed. More females (53%) were in employment compared to males (41%). Wage employment accounts for 54% (47% female, 61% male) of the employment the youth are engaged in while 46% (53% female, 41% male) are self-employed23% (25% female, 22% male) are formally employed while 53% (43% female, 63% male) are in informal employment. Those who work for family ventures account for 25% (33% female, 17% male) of youth who were found to be employed.Income for youth 18-30 years: 59% mainly earn income at a monthly and seasonal frequency. At weekly and daily frequency are 19% and 15% respectively. 19% of the youth indicated that they were not earning any money.Monthly: 356,391/- (251,009 female, 462,325 male) from all sourcesMonthly: 255,897/- (236,860 female, 274,477male) from agriculture The self-employed youth earn more (UGX329,689/-) than their wage employed counterparts (UGX260,945/-).Ownership of assets:The current average value of the assets owned by the youth is UGX12,442,114/- (UGX8,049,870/- female; UGX16,262,842/- male) with value of assets owned by male youth double that of females. Most of the assets are acquired through purchase (86%) and family inheritance (25%). Only a small fraction is acquired through donations (5%), bank loans (2%) and support from projects (1%). Engagement in community groups:70% of the youth are engaged in at least one community group. More female (75%) than male (65%) are members of community groups.Legal status of agribusinesses: 14% of agripreneurship ventures are formally registered. title.narrative: IO 4.3: Evidence-based reforms in agri-skilling and agribusiness management conducted leveraging on action research

description.narrative: The development ecosystem is congested with actors applying different approaches or models to achieve common objectives/goals. It is always a dilemma to choose which of the approaches is most effective unless there is scientifically sound evidence to guide any decisions on which approach or model to use. In the agri-skilling and agribusiness thematic areas such approaches exist and stakeholders face the same challenges when choosing the ones to apply. The SAY project plans to conduct one action research on important aspects and agri-skilling and another one on youth employment in agribusiness. This will provide vital data and information to guide stakeholders across the board when designing and implementing agri-skilling and job creation interventions for youth, a tangible contribution to the agri-skilling and job creation enabling environment.

title.narrative: IO 4.1: Targeted Government of Uganda Ministries, Departments and Agencies operationalized agri-skilling and job creation policies and systemic reforms

description.narrative: The direct involvement of specific government ministries namely Agriculture (for policy guidance, specialized technical services, linkage of youth to government programs and absorption of skilled youth into extension service schemes), education (for skills development related linkages and support), and gender labour and social development (under which youth and employment issues fall) are required not only for the creation of enabling environment but for the execution of processes and attaining results of project interventions. In order for agri-skilling reforms to yield expected results as indicated in the Technical and Vocational Education and Training policy (2019-2024), the mandated body (Agriculture Sector Skills Council) to lead the reforms must implement the planned reform interventions. SAY project plans to facilitate the ASSC in the implementation of these reform interventions. The ASSC will in turn support the skilling process of the project. The MAAIF is agriculture mother ministry and the project aims to engage MAAIF for agribusiness and extension policy popularization, integration of trained youth into extension service provision, technical service provision in training of plant doctors and linking of project beneficiaries to government programs. The project also plans to engage Ministry of Trade, Industry and Cooperative and specifically Uganda Industrial Research Institute to provide Business Incubation Management Services to the young people and other incubators, UNBS for certification of youth products, URSBS and URA for business formalization of youth led agribusinesses. Achieving the desired outcomes from the targeted interventions with government bodies will directly contribute to a favourable enabling environment for youth engagement in agriculture.

description.narrative: The dynamic and fluid nature of the world of work in the twenty first century means new dimensions or requirements are added to jobs at regular intervals and job holders or those seeking will need to have the skills to be competently perform in the jobs. For the training centers to contribute to this trend and ensure that entrants into the job market have the demanded soft and technical skills, it is paramount to renew the training delivery model at regular intervals. In the SKY project analysis of wage employment showed that youth employed at occupation levels 2 and 3 earned well above the UGX 300,000/= (€70) mark and experienced a more positive change in socio-economic status that those employed at level 1. For this reason, SAY project will concentrate on skilling youth at level 2 and 3 and for these ATPs need to be reviewed or developed for use in the project and nationally. This process will require the involvement of public and private sector actors as well as youth so that the final product is acceptable by all and readily adopted for skills development. This will go a long way to reform skilling and contribute to the enabling environment.

title.narrative: Youth highly skilled and gainfully employed in the agriculture sector in Uganda

description.narrative: The project intends to have an impact on the agri-skills level of youth in Uganda and their gainful employment and this will be contributed to by 4 main high-level outcomes which are the specific objectives of the project. in the SKY project 5,519 youth 18-30 years out of 6,763 (82%) equipped with agripreneurship skills attained gainful employment in the agriculture sector (data from the period progress monitoring report of the project). An additional 4,208 youth 13<18 years in secondary schools acquired agripreneurship skills too. In the new project the intention is to increase the number to 10,000 youth to be skilled for immediate employment and 5,000 youth below 18 years for engagement in agribusiness as career choice path or main economic activity.

title.narrative: The project narrative report for 2021
Overall % of youth 13<30 years highly skilled and gainfully employed in agriculture sector in Uganda

description.narrative: Number of youth skilled by the project in the 13<18 and 18-30 years categories employed in agriculture and earning at least €120/person/month divided by the total enrollment target (15,000)

comment.narrative: In the first 6 months of the SAY project, AVSI has executed start-up activities aimed at establishing a strong foundations, system, framework and a technical team that will deliver the expected results of the project. As per the Theory of Change of the project, a set of interrelated interventions clustered into themes will have to be executed inorder to trigger the change process and cause-effect sequences that will lead to the desired outcomes of the project. Key programming lessons learnt from the SKY project informed establishment of these thematic areas. Private Sector Development (PSD) was merged with Business Development for form Agribusiness and PSD. Gender Mainstream and Climate Smart Agriculture that were crosscutting areas in SKY were upgraded into core thematic areas because of their importance for the achievement of the SAY results. A new thematic area Agri-financing, Markets and Linkages was introduced to take care of linking the youth to core service points and resources namely financing, markets and job opportunities. Communications is another thematic area that has been inserted into the SAY project with close linkages to MEAL to ensure a more effective communication of results and packaging of various outputs of the project. Skills Development, and Monitoring Evaluation Accountability and Learning (MEAL), are old thematic areas that have remained untouched but improved programmatically.In the year 2021, the project target of youth gaining employment was 1340 out of 3,200 targeted for skilling. This 1,340 split into 1040 going into agripreneurship (self-employment) and 300 into wage employment within the agriculture sector. Assessment of gainful employment has been set at 6 months after starting a venture or wage employment and the project earning lower limit is set at 120 euros (equivalent to 500,000 UGX). As active skilling commenced in the second quarter of 2021, there were 333 beneficiaries in employment by the end of the year with less than 30% in employment for more than 4 months.

title.narrative: Technical Standards and Strategies developed and approved

description.narrative: The project thematic specialists developed technical standards and strategies that will be rolled out to all partners and used for skilling and executing all implementation processes of the SAY project.

title.narrative: Number of technical references and strategies developed and approved by the project PMU

description.narrative: The standards and strategies are developed participatorily by thematic themes within the SAY project, inputs sought from contemporaries within the sector, experts peer review the developed materials and the PMU approves final document.

comment.narrative: The various technical teams in their working groups comprised of AVSI staff and external experts used the lessons learnt from the SKY project, prevail circumstances in the current Ugandan context, emerging trends and best programming practices, and recommendations from the final evaluation of SKY and Tracer Study of SKY graduates to design standard programming procedures (SPPs) of the SAY project in the form of strategies. Each thematic area’s strategy was appraised and peer-reviewed by respected actors before they were adopted by the SAY PMU for utilization in the project. The following strategies/models have been developed and adopted for use in SAY project:Agribusiness and Private Sector Development StrategySkills Development StrategyClimate Smart Agriculture StrategyGender Mainstreaming StrategyAgri-Financing, Market Systems and Linkages StrategyMEAL StrategyCommunication StrategyAVSI’s Earn As You Learn modelSports for Agripreneurship modelMost Significant Change modelThe contextual analysis findings provided further grounds to refine the strategies and what is in place right now is well grounded to the Ugandan context, responsive to the conditions and assumptions on the ground and adaptable to all the different regions and agro-ecological zones to enable the achievement of outputs that will lead to the desired change processes and outcomes.

title.narrative: IO 3.2: Rehabilitated youth chose agriculture as a safe alternative livelihood

description.narrative: This outcome is proposed for children in rehabilitation providing them with basic agripreneurship skills that can help them to start own enterprises after being released. At the same time, the focus will be in changing their mindset so that through agriculture they can better reintegrate themselves into their community. The community will be also more likely to accept them as they become productive and active members of the society. The period children take in remand homes is variable and so specific and tailored strategy will be adopted in order to cover as broad as possible all the soft and agribusiness entrepreneurial skills. This will equip them with adequate capacity to into simple self-employment. Those who will stay for a period above 3 months can consider to undertake short courses and being assessed by DIT. In this way, together with a new mindset and basic agripreneurship skills, they will be able to acquire a valid certificate which will help them once they reintegrate themselves into their community. The cost for undertake the DIT assessment will be entirely covered by the project considering the vulnerability of these youth category. This is a new outcome area that was not implemented directly in SKYThe project targets to reach 1,000 youth 13<18 years children under rehabilitation. Decision will be made on which Rehabilitation centers to engage after assessment and discussions with the Ministry of Gender Labour and Social Development.

title.narrative: Intermediate Outcome (IO) 1.1: Skilled youth demonstrated competence and job-readiness for agribusiness occupations

description.narrative: Youth in the SKY project were able to find employment simply because they had the DIT certificates that clearly indicated their competencies and that aided the decision-making of potential employers to hire them. Assessing and certifying the competence level of youth graduates also guides them and their potential employers on their best fit slots in jobs. AVSI proposes to continue with the certification of the youth on a cost-shared basis with the youth meeting part of the assessment and certification costs. Without doubt, the DIT certificates are tangible to the youth graduates. This outcome is dependent on skilled and certified youth engaging in occupations in agribusiness and excelling. Under SKY youth were skilled in different occupations in agriculture value chain across the four sub regions. The tracer study done indicates that the skilled youth were not earning adequate income from agribusiness due to inadequate skills attained. In the new project youth with be provided with both technical and soft skills through working with public private sector. It is crucial to work with the private sector because it is the highest employer. Different strategies will be employed to ensure that the youth get updated hands on skills and the competence of skilled youth will be assessed by DIT

title.narrative: OP 4.2.2: Youth agripreneurs accessed markets, investment capital and other critical agribusiness services through established private sector-led trade and investment platforms

description.narrative: Youth will be able to access markets, investment capital and other critical agribusiness services for improved productivity. This will be made possible through the establishment of agri-skilling and agribusiness multi-stakeholder platforms aimed at strengthening public private partnerships for financial inclusion, business development, market access, regulation and enforcement, supplies and technology. In addition, establishing platforms for market system strengthening and linkages between agribusinesses and youth agripreneurs. Capital investment and self-financing model focusing on VSLA and EAYL models. Furthermore, an agribusiness challenge fund will be established where best youth agripreneurs will be rewarded with start-up/scale up funds. Strategic linkages will also be established for youth business capital funding.
